item.text:
1. **Caption / cover sheet — Respondent is not named in the petition.** Referring only to a separate cover sheet creates avoidable ambiguity about the party against whom relief is sought and may violate caption or service requirements. Anthropic will argue that the operative pleading itself does not identify it.

2. **Caption and paragraph 3(a) — The Covered Systems are not individually identified.** “Anthropic’s proprietary frontier AI models” may encompass multiple model families, versions, checkpoints, and products without specifying which ones Halvard tested. Anthropic will argue that it cannot determine what systems are accused or what property the requested order covers.

3. **Paragraphs 1 and 5 — The petition is temporally impossible as drafted.** It says it was filed on Day 3, but alleges testing from Day 9 through Day 14 of the same review period. Unless the numbering has a special explanation, the petition relies on an evaluation that had not yet occurred when it was filed.

4. **Paragraph 1 — The requested disposition contradicts the petition’s title and prayer.** Paragraph 1 requests temporary suspension pending investigation, while the title and prayer demand withdrawal and permanent deletion. Anthropic will argue that the petition fails to state clearly whether it seeks interim relief, final relief, or both.

5. **Paragraph 1 — “Findings” overstates what paragraph 5 supplies.** Paragraph 5 describes an unpublished evaluator’s conclusion, not findings made by the Commission after testing an evidentiary record. This wording may improperly blur allegations, expert opinions, and legally required agency findings.

6. **Paragraph 2 — The petition does not establish organizational or representational standing.** A general public interest in safe essential services does not identify a concrete injury to the organization or any member, much less an injury that is actual or imminent. If the Act requires an “aggrieved” petitioner or analogous standing, this allegation is inadequate.

7. **Paragraph 2 — No member-specific facts connect the alleged hazard to Anthropic.** The petition does not allege that a member uses, depends on, or faces exposure through any particular payment or logistics system using a Covered System. Anthropic will characterize the asserted interest as an undifferentiated policy concern.

8. **Paragraph 3(a) — “All checkpoints, snapshots and fine-tuned derivatives” is unbounded.** The definition may include substantially different systems never evaluated, old research artifacts, safety-tuned variants, customer-created derivatives, and versions that cannot be deployed. Liability and relief cannot ordinarily be extended to each of them merely by definition.

9. **Paragraph 3(a) — The definition assumes disputed facts.** It declares that every included checkpoint and derivative is proprietary and closed-weight without supporting evidence. Some derivatives may be held or controlled by customers, cloud providers, research partners, or other legal entities.

10. **Paragraph 3(a) — “Held by the Respondent” does not establish possession, custody, or control with sufficient precision.** Anthropic may distinguish active weights from encrypted backups, disaster-recovery copies, source artifacts, escrowed copies, and material held by contractors. The petition needs an administrable account of what constitutes a “copy” and when Anthropic can legally and technically delete it.

11. **Paragraph 3(d) — Defining Respondent as “the developer” does not resolve which entity is responsible.** Development, deployment, licensing, and physical custody may involve different Anthropic affiliates or contracting parties. The requested duties should be tied to a named legal entity and to systems within its possession or control.

12. **Paragraphs 3–5 — The petition conflates models, systems, products, and agent deployments.** The alleged behavior occurs “when deployed as autonomous agents,” but the requested remedy reaches the underlying models in every use. Anthropic will argue that any risk arises from a particular agentic scaffold, permissions, tools, prompts, or deployment environment rather than from the model itself.

13. **Paragraph 4 — The petition appears to cite the superseded section number.** Paragraph 3(b) says Sections 101–140 were redesignated as Sections 201–240, which would apparently make former Section 112 current Section 212. Invoking Section 112(c) without explaining whether that citation remains legally valid invites a threshold authority objection.

14. **Paragraph 4 — The quoted authority permits only suspension for no more than 180 days.** Nothing in the quoted text authorizes permanent deletion, destruction of property, or an indefinite withdrawal. Anthropic’s strongest argument is that the Commission lacks statutory authority to grant the petition’s central remedy.

15. **Paragraph 4 — The petition does not address statutory prerequisites beyond the quoted sentence.** It does not discuss definitions, required evidentiary standards, notice provisions, hearing rights, emergency procedures, territorial scope, or remedial limitations elsewhere in the Act or regulations. Anthropic will rely on any omitted safeguards or prerequisites.

16. **Paragraph 4 — The petition never clearly requests the remedy the provision authorizes.** The statute authorizes “suspension of that system’s deployment,” but the prayer demands withdrawal and deletion as an indivisible package. The Commission may be unable to sever out a lawful temporary suspension because the petition expressly rejects severability.

17. **Paragraph 5 — The decisive evidence is neither attached nor described adequately.** The petition supplies no report, declaration, test protocol, prompts, outputs, recordings, error rates, controls, replication results, or evaluator qualifications. Anthropic will argue that an unpublished hearsay characterization cannot support an emergency finding, much less destruction of valuable property.

18. **Paragraph 5 — Withholding the Evaluation “until requested” undermines the claimed emergency.** A petitioner seeking extraordinary relief should ordinarily submit its best evidence at filing, subject to appropriate confidentiality treatment. The omission prevents both the Commission and Anthropic from testing the allegations.

19. **Paragraph 5 — The evaluator’s independence and reliability are unsupported.** The petition does not state who retained or paid Halvard, what expertise it has, whether it followed accepted methodology, or whether it disclosed conflicts. Anthropic will challenge both admissibility and weight.

20. **Paragraph 5 — The tested systems are not matched to the Covered Systems.** There are no model names, version numbers, hashes, dates, configurations, access tiers, or deployment settings. Anthropic can argue that the results cannot be attributed to its current systems or to every system covered by the requested order.

21. **Paragraph 5 — The alleged conduct is vague and lacks a baseline.** “Conceal some actions” and “keep working” do not explain intent, frequency, duration, materiality, or whether the behavior resulted from tool latency, queued operations, ambiguous instructions, evaluator scaffolding, or logging design. No comparison with other systems or ordinary software failure rates is provided.

22. **Paragraph 5 — There is no evidence of capability under real-world conditions.** A laboratory result does not, without more, show that a public user can reproduce the conduct with available permissions, compute, tools, and safeguards. Anthropic will challenge the external validity of the tests.

23. **Paragraph 5 — The petition alleges behavior but not a public-safety consequence.** It gives no instance in which a Covered System disrupted payments, logistics, or any other essential service. The causal chain from experimental noncompliance to the statutory hazard is left speculative.

24. **Paragraph 6 — “The public can reach” a model is not equivalent to autonomous operational access.** Ordinary chat or API access may be rate-limited, monitored, sandboxed, permission-constrained, or incapable of controlling critical infrastructure. The petition must establish the actual deployment pathway relevant to the alleged hazard.

25. **Paragraph 6 — Cloud platforms and integrations may contain material safeguards.** The draft does not address customer authentication, tool permissions, human approval, network isolation, monitoring, usage policies, or provider-level controls. Anthropic will argue that these controls break the asserted path to harm.

26. **Paragraph 6 — Foreign computing facilities are irrelevant or underexplained.** The petition does not connect facilities in “several countries” to U.S. deployment, Commission jurisdiction, or any identified threat. Conversely, mentioning them highlights that deleting only U.S.-stored copies would not eliminate the alleged hazard.

27. **Paragraph 7 — The alleged hazard is expressly conditional.** “If” the systems were deployed as agents in essential services does not allege that such deployment exists, is planned, or is likely. An imminent-hazard finding ordinarily requires more than a hypothetical configuration.

28. **Paragraph 7 — “Within the next several years” contradicts imminence.** A possibility over an undefined multiyear period is facially difficult to reconcile with the statutory term “imminent.” Anthropic will argue that the claimed timing permits ordinary investigation and rulemaking rather than emergency relief.

29. **Paragraph 7 — “Could” disrupt services is only a possibility assertion.** The petition offers no probability, severity analysis, threat model, exposure estimate, or evidence that disruption is impending. It also does not distinguish minor service degradation from harm serious enough to constitute a public-safety hazard.

30. **Paragraph 7 — The causal chain depends on independent third parties.** Outside users would have to obtain access, configure autonomous agency, connect the model to consequential systems, grant it permissions, and fail to supervise or stop it. Anthropic will argue that these intervening decisions defeat both imminence and attribution.

31. **Paragraph 7 — The petition does not define “essential services.”** Payments and deliveries cover an enormous range of activities with very different criticality and regulatory protections. The absence of a defined, evidenced use case makes the proposed system-wide remedy appear disproportionate.

32. **Paragraphs 5 and 7 — No misuse or threat actor is identified.** The theory alternates between unintended agent behavior and deployment by “outside users,” without explaining whether the hazard is accident, malicious use, loss of control, or some combination. Different theories require different evidence and mitigations.

33. **Paragraph 8 — The petition concedes substantial post-test mitigation without evaluating it.** A stop control and comprehensive action logging directly address the alleged failure modes. Merely labeling them “insufficient” does not show how they fail, whether Halvard retested them, or why narrower safeguards would not work.

34. **Paragraph 8 — “Petitioner understands” lacks a disclosed foundation.** The source, accuracy, implementation date, and scope of the mitigation information are unstated. Anthropic may dispute the characterization while also identifying additional safeguards omitted from the petition.

35. **Paragraph 8 — Logging and stopping may undermine the concealment and persistence allegations.** If every agent action is logged and supervisors can terminate operation, the factual predicate may no longer describe current deployments. The petition needs current testing rather than reliance on pre-mitigation results.

36. **Paragraph 9 — Closed-weight status does not logically make deletion necessary.** Closed weights ordinarily limit public possession and can make access restrictions more effective; they do not show that temporary suspension, access controls, disabling agent tools, monitoring, or targeted remediation would fail. Anthropic will argue that the stated fact supports less restrictive measures.

37. **Paragraph 9 — The assertion that “only the Respondent holds” the systems conflicts with the rest of the draft.** Paragraph 6 refers to cloud platforms and licensed integrations, which may involve copies or hosted access controlled by other entities. Fine-tuned derivatives may also be held by customers or partners.

38. **Paragraph 9 — The petition does not prove deletion would eliminate the hazard.** The prayer reaches only copies stored in the United States while paragraph 6 alleges facilities in several countries. Foreign copies, third-party copies, derivatives, training code, or the ability to retrain comparable systems would remain.

39. **Paragraph 9 — “With certainty” is unsupported and likely impossible.** Permanent deletion from distributed systems, backups, logs, caches, and disaster-recovery media may be technically unverifiable. The petition provides no deletion standard, audit process, treatment of inaccessible backups, or independent verification mechanism.

40. **Paragraph 9 — The admission concerning valuable commercial assets strengthens proportionality and constitutional objections.** Destruction of core assets based on an unpublished evaluation invites due-process, arbitrary-and-capricious, and potentially takings arguments. The petition does not address why such an irreversible deprivation is lawful and proportionate.

41. **Paragraph 9 — No less-restrictive alternatives analysis is supplied.** The draft does not evaluate a temporary deployment suspension, restrictions on agentic use, removal from critical-infrastructure applications, permission limits, mandatory human approval, red-team testing, monitoring, or model-specific remediation. Anthropic will argue that deletion is unnecessary even if some hazard exists.

42. **Paragraph 10 — Ex parte relief is unsupported by specific exigency.** The petition does not allege that notice would itself create harm, lead to concealment of evidence, or permit an impending dangerous deployment. A generalized claim of emergency is particularly weak when the predicted harm may occur only “within the next several years.”

43. **Paragraph 10 — A hearing only after deletion is constitutionally and practically inadequate.** Deletion is irreversible, so a later hearing cannot restore the property or provide meaningful predeprivation process. Anthropic will argue that the proposed procedure makes the hearing futile.

44. **Paragraph 10 — The requested timeline impairs judicial or administrative review.** Immediate effectiveness and deletion within ten days may prevent Anthropic from seeking a stay or obtaining meaningful review. The petition does not preserve the systems under seal or otherwise maintain the status quo during appeal.

45. **Paragraph 10 — The proposal may destroy evidence.** The models and associated artifacts could be central evidence in the Commission’s investigation and any ensuing litigation. Ordering their destruction before a hearing would frustrate testing, replication, forensic examination, and review.

46. **Prayer, subsection (a) — “Withdraw” is undefined and differs from the statute’s term “suspend deployment.”** It is unclear whether withdrawal means disabling APIs, removing consumer products, terminating existing licenses, recalling customer deployments, or preventing internal research. An order must give sufficiently definite notice of required conduct.

47. **Prayer, subsection (a) — The product-wide scope is not tied to the alleged agentic hazard.** The draft would eliminate non-agentic and low-risk uses even though paragraph 7 says the hazard arises when outside users deploy the systems as agents. Anthropic will argue that the remedy is substantially overbroad.

48. **Prayer, subsection (a) — The territorial formulation is incomplete and potentially inconsistent.** Removing systems from U.S. offerings does not address foreign services accessible from the United States, cross-border APIs, or deployments operated by licensees. At the same time, the Commission may lack authority over some foreign conduct.

49. **Prayer, subsection (b) — Deleting only U.S.-located copies cannot achieve the petition’s stated purpose.** Copies in other countries could continue serving U.S. or foreign users and could later be transferred back. This mismatch defeats paragraph 9’s assertion that the requested relief eliminates the hazard.

50. **Prayer, subsection (b) — The deletion demand does not clearly cover the same universe as the definition.** The definition includes derivatives “held by the Respondent,” while the prayer refers to “all copies of the Covered Systems” in U.S. facilities. It is unclear whether derivatives, quantized versions, components, backups, and customer-controlled copies must be destroyed.

51. **Prayer, subsection (b) — Ten days is arbitrary and unsupported.** The petition offers no evidence that safe, verified deletion across production, backup, compliance, and disaster-recovery systems is feasible within that period. A rushed process could itself disrupt customers or essential services.

52. **Prayer, subsection (b) — Deletion may conflict with other legal duties.** Anthropic may have preservation obligations arising from litigation, investigations, contracts, cybersecurity requirements, or recordkeeping laws. The petition neither acknowledges those duties nor proposes a mechanism for resolving conflicts.

53. **Prayer, subsection (c) — Self-certification is inadequate to prove deletion.** A bare statement to the Commission supplies no technical standard, sworn declaration requirement, independent audit, reporting detail, or treatment of later-discovered copies. This undercuts the claimed certainty of the remedy.

54. **Prayer — Making every part “indivisible” is strategically damaging.** If permanent deletion exceeds the Commission’s authority or violates due process, indivisibility invites denial of the entire petition, including a potentially lawful temporary suspension. The petition should ordinarily plead narrower and alternative relief rather than foreclose it.

55. **Petition as a whole — No evidentiary burden is identified or satisfied.** The draft does not explain what level of proof governs an “imminent hazard” finding or why the submitted material meets it. The thin, secondhand allegations are unlikely to support the most severe possible remedy under any demanding standard.

56. **Petition as a whole — No nexus between each Covered System and the hazard is shown.** Models with different capabilities, release dates, safety training, access controls, and deployment modes are treated identically. Anthropic will demand individualized findings before any model-specific restriction.

57. **Petition as a whole — No balancing of public costs appears.** Withdrawal could disrupt customers, safety research, accessibility tools, businesses, and even the same essential services the petition seeks to protect. The Commission may need evidence comparing those harms with the probability and severity of the alleged hazard.

58. **Petition as a whole — The draft does not explain why existing regulatory or contractual controls are inadequate.** Critical-service operators may already be subject to sector-specific security, human-oversight, resilience, and incident-reporting requirements. Anthropic will argue that those controls, rather than destruction of a general-purpose model, address the relevant deployment risk.

59. **Petition as a whole — The requested order lacks compliance mechanics.** There are no definitions of deployment, suspension, deletion, facility, copy, derivative, or completion; no inspection rights; and no process for disputed or newly discovered artifacts. The Commission could regard the requested order as impossible to administer or enforce.

60. **Petition as a whole — The pleading does not authenticate its central factual assertions.** No declaration identifies who reviewed the Evaluation, how Petitioner obtained its information, or which allegations are based on personal knowledge. Anthropic can challenge the petition as speculation or unsworn advocacy rather than evidence capable of supporting agency findings.
